# Exclusive: Plantik and Hudson River Biotechnology team up to de-risk heat-tolerant strawberries
...
#### Lotte Westerhof, CSO of Hudson River Biotechnology, with Plantik cofounder Ying Shao. Image credit: Plantik Biosciences
Plantik Biosciences and Hudson River Biotechnology are partnering to develop heat tolerance in crops, with the goal of producing a validated heat-tolerance trait any strawberry breeder can license.
By combining heat-tolerant targets identified and validated by Plantik in tomatoes with “transgene-free” strawberry genome editing methods developed by Hudson River, the companies hope to turn trait discoveries into “improved strawberry varieties.”
Validation trials are already underway.
According to Plantik cofounder and CEO Ying Shao, heat tolerance is “a must-have trait for many crops across the globe” thanks to the rise in extreme heat events worldwide in recent years.
Strawberries are among the most exposed crops, as these high temperatures disrupt flowering and fruit set, and damage overall fruit quality.
...
#### Performance under high heat
France-based Plantik employs its ATLANTIS machine learning platform to search “the dark genome,” the regulatory stretches of DNA in plants that switch genes on and off.
It then edits those regions without inserting any foreign DNA, allowing plant breeders to fast-track development of crops.
Plantik’s first product is a heat-tolerant tomato, which the company claims it developed in about 12 months instead of the five to eight years required by traditional breeding.
The company is currently running demonstrations across greenhouses and fields in the US and Belgium.
“We have now worked on this trait in multiple tomato crops, from lab tomatoes to now commercial hybrids,” says Shao.
...
#### Editing at speed
Hudson River says its BioMaas platform gives breeders access to genome editing without the time and expense of building the R&D in-house.
Thus far the company has focused on tomatoes and strawberries.
“We have now developed technical capabilities that allow us to very rapidly deploy new traits in those crops, like the heat-tolerant trait,” says Hudson River CEO Fernando Los.
He adds that the company can now make complex edits in these crops “in a matter of months.”
Changes to EU rules, which simplify CRISPR regulations, have also caused “a surge of interest” in the business.
Los says the open nature of the Hudson River platform is the company’s biggest differentiator.
Breeders get the technology plus a range of traits, including new proprietary traits like heat tolerance.
Third-party trait developers such as Plantik get access to Hudson River’s network of breeders.
In this specific partnership, BioMass will act “as a bridge” between trait innovators like Plantik and breeders.
Beginning with strawberries, Plantik will identify which parts of the genome to edit for heat tolerance, and Hudson River makes those edits in the plants.
“Strawberry is a different story from tomato because it’s genetically much more complex,” says Los.
“It’s an octoploid species rather than a diploid.
Propagation is normally done clonaly, so you cannot create seeds; you have to work directly in relevant commercial germplasm, which are all things that we can do.”
Strawberry is the starting point, and the companies plan to take the approach to other crops later.
They are also inviting other companies to bring trait challenges for their own strawberry varieties.
...
#### De-risking heat tolerance for breeders
Strawberry breeders have it hardest, he adds, because they lack the resources to run a full genome editing workflow in-house.
“What we offer here is essentially de-risking and very cheap access to a piece of technology that’s normally only available to the very largest companies,” says Los.
“If you reduce the failure rate from 90% to maybe 10% for a breeder, that’s a very good proposition to offer them.”

# ENGINEERING RESILIENT PLANTS FASTER
Plantik develops technologies to recover trait and crop diversity vital for a resilient future.
We make it faster, because there is no time to wait.
#### Our Plant Engineering Platform
# ATLANTIS
### THE DARK GENOME UNLOCKED
With the ATLANTIS™ platform, we answer the ultimate question: **Where should we look at?**
ATLANTIS™ is built on the latest cloud data infrastructure to analyze, discover, and formulate the best strategies to generate trait variations.
It makes it possible to explore *the Dark Genome* of the plant, which allows minimal, precise changes to fine-tune gene expression for complex, quantitative traits.
#### Our (Dark) Genome Editing Tool
# PROEDIT
### AN ADVANCED WORKFLOW
Combined with the targets found using ATLANTIS™, our advanced (dark) genome editing workflow enables precise and effective delivery of the chosen CRISPR machinery.
Our protocols will bring this breakthrough technology to emerging and diverse crops to increase the resilience of our food system.
# THERMO-TOLERANCE
Thermotolerance is the ability of a plant to withstand and survive high temperatures.
Temperature fluctuations can negatively impact plant growth and reduce yield.
Plantik is dedicated to increasing plant’s resilience under heat stress.

# 8 AI Players to Watch in Crop Breeding
## Plantik Biosciences
Based in: France
Rather than making changes to genes that encode protein, Plantik Biosciences targets the non-coding genes that regulate when and how rigorously a gene functions.
Making changes to this ‘regulatory DNA’ enables plants to increase the strength of their response to heat, drought or disease, but permanent activation of stress responses (which can carry a yield or growth penalty) is avoided.
Plantik’s AI system uses multi-omic data to identify regulatory genetic switches and conduct edits using the chosen CRISPR approach, with an initial focus on tomatoes, corn and soybeans.
The business model has a long-term focus on developing traits in-house and licensing them to seed companies, while making revenue in the near term by providing various services.
Plantik’s co-founders were named in the “Palmarès des inventeurs” at the Paris-Saclay Summit in February 2026.

# Hudson River and Plantik partner to enhance heat tolerance in strawberries
...
#### Hudson River Biotechnology (HRB) Netherlands
Plant genome-editing technology company Hudson River and plant engineering company Plantik announced a partnership to bring heat tolerance into commercial strawberries.
The programme combines heat-tolerance targets identified and validated by Plantik in tomato with the transgene-free strawberry genome-editing methods developed by Hudson River to translate trait discoveries into improved strawberry varieties.
...
Strawberry is among the most exposed to high temperatures, disrupting its flowering and fruit set, reducing yield and negatively impacting fruit quality.
Plantik brings demonstrated expertise in engineering heat tolerance - validated in tomato across multiple genetic backgrounds with field demonstrations currently under way across multiple locations in the US and Europe.
This is combined with Hudson River’s proprietary, transgene-free genome-editing method, already tailored to strawberry and well suited for complex traits such as heat tolerance.
Together, the two companies plan to improve heat tolerance in strawberries and help breeders protect both productivity and marketable fruit quality given increasingly challenging growing conditions.
*"Heat tolerance has become a must-have trait for many crops across the globe.
Plants' ability to withstand increasingly intensified and repeated heatwaves while preserving yield will continue to be a top priority in the coming years,″ said Ying Shao, Co-Founder and CEO of Plantik.*
The partnership brings together unique technologies developed by each company.
Plantik’s ATLANTIS platform offers proprietary discovery capabilities to identify high-potential targets for engineering complex traits without compromise.
Hudson River’s BioMaas platform enables breeders to access its advanced genome-editing capabilities without having to build the R&D and technology in-house.
Throughout this collaboration, BioMaas will act as a bridge between trait innovators and breeders – helping trait companies translate their discoveries into crop-specific applications, while giving breeders an accessible route to valuable new traits.
Through BioMaas, strawberry breeders will be able to access unique and proprietary traits from specialized discovery companies such as Plantik, helping them expand and accelerate their innovation pipelines.
The partnership will tackle the heat tolerance challenge in strawberries as a starting point before applying it in other crops.
*″This collaboration is a perfect example of how trait knowledge can be leveraged from one crop to another, without the trait needing to be present in the breeder’s germplasm or lengthy backcrossing and selection.
With BioMaas, we introduce the desired trait directly into elite germplasm, creating material ready for commercialisation in a single generation,″ said Lotte Westerhof, CSO of Hudson River.*
Validation trials are already underway between the two companies, who are welcoming trait challenges from companies looking to implement these into their strawberry varieties.

Plantik’s proprietary cloud data infrastructure and machine learning platform ATLANTIS has been pivotal to the work, Shao added.

hits.title: Two Biotechs Edit Strawberries' "Dark Genome" to Survive Hotter Summers
hits.snippet:
# Two Biotechs Edit Strawberries’ “Dark Genome” to Survive Hotter Summers
**29 September 2026, Netherlands:** Two European agricultural biotech companies, Plantik Biosciences of France and Hudson River Biotechnology of the Netherlands, announced on September 28 that they are extending a gene-editing partnership from tomatoes into strawberries, targeting heat tolerance as extreme temperature events become more frequent across major growing regions.
The announcement was first reported by AgFunderNews, and validation trials on the edited strawberry material are already underway.
The two companies bring complementary pieces of the same puzzle.
Plantik, based at the Genopole biotech cluster near Paris, has built a machine learning platform called ATLANTIS that scans what scientists call the “dark genome,” the large share of a plant’s DNA that does not directly code for proteins but instead controls when, where and how strongly nearby genes switch on.
Rather than searching for a single gene to disable or insert, ATLANTIS is designed to identify small tweaks to these regulatory regions that adjust a plant’s existing traits without introducing foreign DNA.
Hudson River Biotechnology, based at Wageningen Campus in the Netherlands, supplies the execution side through its BioMaas platform, which performs the actual genome edits in crop tissue using transgene-free methods, meaning the final plant carries no inserted genetic material from another species, only altered versions of its own DNA sequence.
...
## From Tomato to Strawberry
The strawberry project builds directly on an earlier collaboration between the two companies that produced a heat-tolerant tomato line.
According to the companies, that tomato was developed in roughly 12 months using the ATLANTIS-BioMaas combination, compared with the five to eight years a conventional breeding program would typically need to introduce and stabilize a similar trait.
The edited tomato has since shown improved yield preservation under high-heat conditions in real-world trial settings, according to the companies, giving them a proof point to apply the same approach to a new crop.
Strawberries present a different breeding challenge than tomatoes.
Commercial strawberry varieties are complex, high-value fruiting plants that are typically propagated clonally rather than from seed, and heat stress during flowering and fruit set can sharply cut both yield and fruit quality, a problem already visible in strawberry-growing regions from California to southern Europe during recent hot growing seasons.
Plantik cofounder and chief executive Ying Shao said heat tolerance has become “a must-have trait for many crops across the globe” as extreme heat events grow more common, a rationale that applies as much to fruit and vegetable crops as to the row crops that have historically received more breeding investment.
...
## Live Newsroom
Neither company disclosed financial terms of the expanded partnership or named specific funding behind the strawberry work.
...
The approach illustrated by this partnership, editing regulatory DNA rather than protein-coding genes, is part of a broader shift in plant biotechnology that regulators in several markets, including the European Union and India, have begun treating differently from conventional transgenic GM crops, since no foreign gene is inserted into the final plant.
That distinction matters commercially: precision-bred or gene-edited varieties of this kind can often reach farmers faster and with a lighter regulatory path than first-generation GM crops, which is part of why venture-backed biotechs are racing to apply the model across specialty and fruit crops, not just the commodity row crops that dominated the first wave of agricultural biotechnology.

“It’s an octoploid species rather than a diploid.
Propagation is normally done clonaly, so you cannot create seeds; you have to work directly in relevant commercial germplasm, which are all things that we can do.”
The collaboration is designed to reduce the technical and financial risks faced by breeders seeking to introduce complex traits.

...

Strawberries are only the starting point.
Plantik and Hudson River plan to apply the same model to other crops and are inviting companies to bring additional trait challenges for strawberry varieties.
If the validation process succeeds, the partnership could create a pathway for breeders to access **genome-editing technology and climate-resilience traits** without developing the entire technological platform themselves, accelerating the introduction of new varieties designed for hotter growing conditions.

For seed companies, nurseries and horticultural input suppliers serving strawberry and other high-value fruit sectors in India, the Gulf and Southeast Asia, where rising temperatures are already squeezing flowering and fruit-set windows, a validated method for compressing trait development from years to months is a preview of how climate-adaptation traits may increasingly reach the market.

# Exogenous regulators enhance strawberry yield under heat stress conditions
Sci Rep. 2026 Jan 16;16(1):5573.
doi: 10.1038/s41598-026-35730-z.
...
## Abstract
This study evaluated the effectiveness of different exogenous chemical treatments in enhancing heat stress tolerance across three strawberry genotypes RABI-3, BARI Strawberry-2, and BARI Strawberry-3 under prolonged summer conditions in Bangladesh.
A two-factorial completely randomized design (CRD) was conducted from February 2024 to April 2025 with six treatments: control (water), abscisic acid (5 ppm), calcium chloride (10 mM), kaolin (5%), melatonin (10 ppm), and molasses (5%).
Vegetative, physiological, biochemical, and yield parameters were analyzed, and treatment effects were statistically tested at 5% significance level.
Kaolin application significantly improved vegetative growth (plant height and leaf number increased by 15-25% compared to the control) and enhanced photosynthetic activity and antioxidant capacity.
The kaolin treated plants also showed a 20-30% yield increase with better fruit size, total soluble solids, and vitamin C content.
Among genotypes, BARI Strawberry-3 demonstrated the highest tolerance and yield stability under high-temperature stress.These findings suggest that kaolin spray may offer a cost effective and environmentally sustainable approach to mitigating heat stress in strawberries, with BARI Strawberry-3 representing a promising genotype for future commercial cultivation in warming agro-climatic zones.

# Plantik Biosciences and heat-tolerant strawberries — investigation cut-off: **20 October 2026**

## Bottom line

**Plantik Biosciences is a small, independent French SAS whose verified legal entity is PLANTIK BIOSCIENCES, SIREN 853 088 441, and whose official domain is `plantik.bio`.** No parent, controlled subsidiary, alternate legal entity, Chinese affiliate, or acquired company was established in this research pass. Its registered office is in Orléans; its Paris office and Genopole laboratory are operating locations rather than separate companies. [16]

**Its strawberry program is genuinely a genome-editing program—not conventional breeding—but remains precommercial.** Announced on **28 September 2026**, it combines Plantik’s ATLANTIS target-discovery work and tomato heat-tolerance evidence with Hudson River Biotechnology’s transgene-free, protoplast-based strawberry editing/regeneration platform. The parties said validation trials were already underway, but they disclosed no strawberry line name, edit sequence, target gene, quantitative heat result, independent replication, regulator submission, commercial breeder/germplasm partner, sale, or approval. The intended output is a **validated licensable trait**, not yet a finished strawberry cultivar. [31][204]

The strongest publicly disclosed evidence belongs to Plantik’s **tomato**, not strawberry: controlled heat-wave proof of concept, multi-genotype work, 2026 greenhouse/field demonstrations in Florida, elsewhere in the US, and Belgium, plus a US regulatory inquiry for promoter-edited tomato germplasm. Transferring the trait concept from tomato into octoploid strawberry remains an announced and reportedly trial-stage hypothesis—not a demonstrated commercial strawberry trait. [145][196][200]

---

## 1. Identity, domain, aliases and corporate structure

| Legal name | **PLANTIK BIOSCIENCES** | Incorporated 15 Jul 2019; RCS registration 8 Aug 2019 | French registry-derived record: “Dénomination / nom légal: PLANTIK BIOSCIENCES.” [16] | https://www.pappers.fr/entreprise/plantik-biosciences-853088441 |

### Capital and ownership caveat

Registered capital rose from **€82 at formation**, to **€820 in 2022**, and then to **€1,479.49 by 20 September 2026**. That nominal capital is not the same thing as cumulative investment or valuation. The August 2026 filings record several new-share issuances, but public beneficial-owner information does not reveal who subscribed; therefore the 2026 increase cannot safely be attributed to a named investor. [16]

---

## 2. What Plantik actually does: editing versus breeding

| Technology or term | What the evidence establishes | Editing, conventional breeding, or enabling technology? | Demonstration level by cut-off | Supporting excerpt / source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **ATLANTIS** | Cloud/data and machine-learning platform combining genomic or multi-omic information to find regulatory “dark genome” targets controlling traits | **Target discovery**, not itself an editing enzyme or breeding method | Used to nominate targets; tomato is the disclosed proof point | Plantik describes modifying “small and precise targets in the under-explored ‘dark genome’”; AgFunder reports ATLANTIS searches regulatory DNA that switches genes on/off. [2][31] |
| Dark-genome/promoter editing | Plantik targets non-coding regulatory DNA rather than necessarily disrupting a protein-coding gene | **Genome editing**, reportedly without foreign DNA in the final plant | Tomato demonstrated; strawberry only in partnership validation | USDA filing says the final tomato “contains no foreign DNA” and describes CRISPR/Cas-mediated promoter deletion. [145][213] |
| CRISPR/Cas | Plantik’s tomato regulatory filing explicitly says it used CRISPR/Cas-mediated editing; HRB supplies strawberry editing/regeneration | **Genome editing** | Demonstrated in tomato; HRB separately demonstrated edited-cell regeneration in strawberry | Plantik USDA submission: “Plantik is using CRISPR/cas-mediated…” [145] |
| Plant Engineering Workflow / Smart Breeding | Umbrella terminology for target identification, editing, validation and accelerated crop development | **Marketing/workflow term**; should not be treated as conventional breeding alone | Platform/service offering | Genopole lists “identification and validation of genetic targets through different CRISPR genome editing systems” plus genome analysis. [225] |
| Speed breeding | Appears in older descriptions of Plantik’s combined workflow | **Breeding-cycle acceleration**, not proof that a particular product was edited | No strawberry-specific speed-breeding evidence found | Third-party profile describes gene editing, bioinformatics and speed breeding together; it should not be used to infer every program’s exact method. [29] |
| HRB **BioMaas** | Service platform for transgene-free/DNA-free editing and regeneration of elite commercial germplasm | **Genome-editing deployment platform** | Strawberry platform reportedly tested over 30 genotypes | HRB says breeders can access editing without building the technology in-house; Westerhof described testing “more than 30 genotypes.” [320][321] |
| HRB **TiGER** | Workflow regenerating a complete strawberry plant from a single edited cell, with automated screening of regeneration conditions | **Editing/regeneration workflow** | Demonstrated in February 2024 | HRB announced “the world's first successful regeneration of strawberry plants from gene-edited single cells.” [308] |
| HRB hydrogel | Supports individual strawberry protoplasts returning to cell cycle and forming callus | **Regeneration technology** | Claimed operational in strawberry | HRB CSO: “proprietary hydrogel technology” supports protoplast-to-callus development. [321] |
| Pairwise **Fulcrum®** | Editing tools, enzymes and trait libraries licensed to HRB in May 2026 | **Genome-editing IP/platform licence** | Licensed to HRB generally for vegetables, soft fruit and other species | Agreement gave HRB “access to the Fulcrum® plant gene editing platform.” It does **not** say Pairwise co-owns Plantik’s strawberry trait. [338] |
| Conventional crossing | Used by commercial breeders such as PSI/PSG, Planasa and Fall Creek alongside newer tools | **Conventional/advanced breeding** | Extensive commercial variety portfolios | PSI describes “traditional crossing techniques, and other technologies”; Planasa says “a mix of traditional breeding methods and modern technology.” [258][238] |
| Ohalo **Boosted Breeding™** | Changes reproductive inheritance so offspring receive the complete genomes of both parents | Proprietary reproductive/breeding system that can use editing; **not synonymous with CRISPR generally** | Ohalo programs only | Ohalo: offspring “contain all the genes from the mother and all the genes from the father.” Nothing reviewed connects Plantik to Ohalo. [62] |

### Required distinction concerning Boosted Breeding

**Boosted Breeding is Ohalo’s proprietary reproductive system; it is not a generic synonym for CRISPR, promoter editing, gene editing, doubled haploids, F1-hybrid seed, or advanced breeding.** Ohalo says it switches off reproductive circuits so each parent transmits its entire genome. The fact that Ohalo lists “berries” among possible crops does **not** establish that Plantik, HRB, PSI, Simplot, Pairwise, Fall Creek or Planasa uses Boosted Breeding, nor that every company appearing in a berry-industry roster edits berries. [62][68]

No Plantik–Ohalo partnership or Boosted Breeding licence was established in this research pass.

---

## 3. Plantik crops, traits, programs and named products

| Crop/program | Trait or objective | Method publicly established | Stage by 20 Oct 2026 | Named product/line | Geography distinct from HQ | Commercial availability |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Tomato** | Heat tolerance; pollen fertility, flower development, fruit set/yield preservation and potentially pericarp thickness under elevated temperature | CRISPR/Cas promoter editing of a thermomorphogenesis-associated transcription-factor regulatory region; public evidence strongly points to **PIF4-regulatory editing** | Controlled proof of concept completed; work across multiple genetic backgrounds and commercial hybrids; 2026 greenhouse/field demonstrations | No consumer brand or cultivar name disclosed | Florida greenhouse; additional US and Belgium greenhouse/field demonstrations; India and South/Southeast Asia stated as target markets | **Not established**; intended licensing, introgression and eventual commercialization only |
| **Strawberry** | Conditional heat response intended to protect flowering, fruit set, yield and marketable quality without changing normal growth when heat is absent | Plantik ATLANTIS target nomination + HRB transgene-free strawberry editing/regeneration | Partnership announced; “validation trials already underway”; larger/commercial field trials publicly planned for 2028 | **No line, cultivar, event or brand disclosed** | HRB in Wageningen; actual 2026 validation site not disclosed; 2028 trial geography not firmly disclosed | **No** |
| **Potato** | Heat tolerance | Joint venture concept: Plantik trait discovery, SolEdits editing, NYZU funding/commercialization | Announced/joint venture; no named variety or disclosed field result found | “Potato Improver” is project/JV wording, not an established retail cultivar | Sweden-linked partners; intended high-heat markets including India | **Not established** |
| **Quinoa** | Accelerated/resilient breeding | “Modern breeding technologies”; exact edits and targets not publicly specified | Consortium R&D | None disclosed | Netherlands consortium with Wageningen Plant Research, Radicle Crops and Lekker Lupine | **Not established** |
| **White lupin** | Accelerated breeding | Same consortium; do not infer CRISPR without product-level evidence | Consortium R&D | None disclosed | Netherlands | **Not established** |
| **Hemp** | Trait discovery/development | Platform reported as applied to hemp; exact product method not disclosed publicly | R&D | None disclosed | University College Dublin relationship reported by secondary source; precise program location/status not established | **Not established** |
| **Corn/maize** | Regulatory-target datasets / future complex traits | Machine-learning and multi-omic target discovery | Dataset/platform work | None | Not disclosed | **Not established** |
| **Soybean** | Regulatory-target datasets / future complex traits | Machine-learning and multi-omic target discovery | Dataset/platform work | None | Not disclosed | **Not established** |

The company’s own/Genopole descriptions specifically identify hemp, quinoa and tomato as platform applications, while a July 2026 interview added tomato, corn and soybean datasets. These references do not establish edited commercial products in every listed crop. [225][203]

---

## 4. Strawberry heat-tolerance program: claim-by-claim evidence grading

| Claim | Status | Evidence and conflict/gap |
|---|---|---|
| Plantik and HRB formed a strawberry heat-tolerance partnership | **Announced** | Publicly reported 28 September 2026; corroborated by HRB/industry coverage. [31][204] |
| The program uses genome editing | **Established as the intended method** | Plantik identifies regulatory targets; HRB makes the edits using a transgene-free strawberry workflow. [31][266] |
| Strawberry plants have already been edited for Plantik’s heat target | **Reported but details not independently established** | “Validation trials are already underway” implies edited or candidate material exists, but no event, genotype, sequence, image, protocol or data were released. [31] |
| Heat tolerance has been demonstrated in strawberry | **Not established in this research pass** | All public quantitative efficacy evidence found concerns tomato. No strawberry heat-treatment results, controls, yield figures or peer-reviewed data were located. |
| The same exact tomato edit is being made in strawberry | **Not established** | The parties say tomato-validated “targets” provide the starting point, but strawberry orthologue, motif, edit and dosage across eight chromosome sets are undisclosed. |
| The target is strawberry PIF4 | **Plausible inference, not established** | Plantik’s tomato regulatory evidence and the founders’ earlier PIF4 patent point in that direction, but neither company publicly named the strawberry gene. It should not be stated as fact. |
| The edited strawberry is transgene-free | **Program design/HRB claim, not event-level confirmation** | HRB calls its platform transgene-free/DNA-free; no event-specific molecular dossier was public. [321] |
| Normal growth is unchanged without heat | **Design goal/CEO claim, not demonstrated strawberry result** | Ying Shao said the goal is a conditional heat response and normal behavior without stress. No strawberry dataset was disclosed. [14] |
| Multiple elite strawberry genotypes can be edited | **HRB platform demonstration, not Plantik-trait validation** | HRB said it had tested more than 30 genotypes for platform/regeneration performance. That does not mean 30 Plantik heat-tolerant lines. [321] |
| Breeders can license the trait | **Planned business model** | The stated goal is “a validated heat-tolerance trait any strawberry breeder can license.” No executed breeder licence was disclosed. [31] |
| Commercial field trials are underway | **No** | Reports say validation trials are underway; the first larger/commercial field trials were planned for spring/summer **2028**. [14] |
| Commercial fruit is available | **No** | No Plantik/HRB strawberry variety, fruit or planting stock was offered for sale as of the cut-off. |
| Regulatory clearance exists | **No strawberry-specific clearance found** | No USDA, FDA, UK, Canadian, EU or other Plantik/HRB strawberry filing or decision was identified. |
| Heat-tolerant strawberry product name | **Not established** | None announced. |
| Commercial germplasm/breeder partner | **Not established** | “Elite germplasm” is discussed, but the owner/provider is not named. HRB welcomed breeders’ trait challenges; that is not an announced cultivar partner. [204] |

---

## 5. Tomato evidence underpinning the strawberry concept

| Evidence layer | Date | What was demonstrated or claimed | Exact excerpt / attribution | Assessment |
|---|---:|---|---|---|
| Controlled proof of concept | Disclosed 23 Oct 2024 | Edited tomato tolerated a seven-day simulated heat wave; comparator reportedly lost about 30% yield | Ying Shao: “it was not affected by the heat wave and maintained the same yield, whereas the wild plant under the heat lost about 30% yield.” [80] | Company-reported controlled result; no peer-reviewed Plantik paper found |
| Development speed | Disclosed 2024 | Proof of concept in about 12 months versus five–eight years claimed for conventional breeding | Plantik/AgFunder: “12 months instead of the five to eight years required by traditional breeding.” [79] | Company comparison; depends on endpoints and is not a head-to-head breeding trial |
| Regulatory dossier evidence | 2025 filing, public by 2026 | Reduced thermomorphogenesis, improved pollen viability/germination, normal flowers, increased fruit set/pericarp thickness in some lines, effect across genotypes | USDA submission enumerates those five experimental observations. [145] | Strongest technical public disclosure, but parts of target/location/data are CBI-redacted |
| Florida demonstration | 26 May 2026 | Multiple edited lines growing under greenhouse production conditions; heat tests forthcoming | Plantik: tomatoes “officially live in Florida” and “will soon undergo the first heat stress tests.” [191] | Establishes planting, not yet outcome at announcement date |
| Multi-location demonstrations | Summer 2026 | Greenhouse and field demonstrations in US and Belgium; commercial-hybrid backgrounds | Shao: “from lab tomatoes to now commercial hybrids”; “performs much better in terms of yield preservation under high heat.” [web:196
